notes.title: Start here: a small subscription-billing API
notes.body:
This repo is a Stripe-style subscription billing dashboard: Billing.Api is a .NET 8 minimal API with in-memory storage, background workers for payments and outbound webhooks, and Billing.Web is the front end. This pack uses two short design notes in **docs/**:

1. **docs/architecture.md**: the backend layout, the money representation, idempotency and background jobs. Read its status box first; it records what the original note left out.
2. **docs/webhooks.md**: how inbound payment-provider webhooks are verified, and what the endpoint does not do.

Both notes are short, so the real work is in the code they point to: WebhookSignatureVerifier, IdempotencyMiddleware, Money, BillingEngine and the endpoint definitions in Program.cs. The status box also warns that main does not compile as committed; you do not need to build anything for this pack, only to read.

excerpts.quote: `Billing.Api` is a dependency-free .NET 8 minimal API.

readMore.why: Every endpoint and the service registrations in one file.
The backend layout: Domain, Contracts, Infrastructure and Program.cs.

notes.title: Core idea: signed webhooks and replay windows
notes.body:
A webhook is an HTTP call from a payment provider to your API. Because anyone can send an HTTP request, the provider signs each one: it computes an HMAC (a keyed hash) over the payload with a secret both sides share, and sends the result in a header. Only a holder of the secret can produce a matching signature. Signing a timestamp together with the body lets the receiver refuse old captured requests, which limits replay.

Read WebhookSignatureVerifier.IsValid and list every condition under which it returns false, in order. For the timestamp check, work out the sign of the subtraction for a timestamp in the past and for one in the future, and compare with what the webhook note says. Look at how both signature strings are prepared before comparison, then look up CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals in the .NET docs and find out which attack it is designed to stop.

Finally, follow the endpoint in Program.cs after verification succeeds: what it stores, what it echoes back, and which engine method it calls.

excerpts.quote: Signed payload: `{timestamp}.{rawBody}`.

readMore.why: The whole signature check in about forty lines.
ApplyPaymentResult: what a payment webhook changes.

notes.title: Core idea: idempotency keys, and money as whole cents
notes.body:
An idempotency key is a client-chosen string sent with an unsafe request so that retrying the same request returns the first result instead of doing the work twice. The architecture note describes the intent; IdempotencyMiddleware is the implementation, about seventy lines.

Read InvokeAsync and draw every path through it as a small flowchart: which requests it skips, what it does when the header is absent, the length rule, what is hashed into the request hash versus what forms the cache key, what happens on a cache hit with the same or a different hash, and exactly when and under what condition store.Set runs. Then ask what two requests arriving together would each see.

For money, the note says amounts are integer minor units plus a currency code. Read Money.FromMajor, the constructor and NormalizeCurrency, and note the rounding mode used and what happens to the currency string.

excerpts.quote: Money is represented as integer minor units plus ISO currency.

readMore.why: The idempotency middleware and its in-memory store.

notes.title: The tolerance only looks backwards
notes.body:
**Key: valid, because only timestamps over five minutes old are rejected.**

The check is `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow - timestamp > TimestampTolerance`. For a timestamp one hour ahead, UtcNow - timestamp is minus one hour, which is never greater than five minutes, so the check passes and, with a correct HMAC, IsValid returns true. The webhook note flags exactly this: a far-future signed request can be replayed indefinitely, and comparing the absolute difference closes it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Both directions**: that needs Math.Abs, which the code does not use.
- **FromUnixTimeSeconds refuses the future**: it accepts any value up to year 9999.
- **Only within five minutes of the clock**: that is the symmetric rule the guide recommends, not the current one.

excerpts.quote: if (DateTimeOffset.UtcNow - timestamp > TimestampTolerance)

notes.title: A failed verification is a 401
notes.body:
**Key: 401, from Results.Unauthorized once IsValid returns false.**

Six minutes is more than the five-minute tolerance, so IsValid returns false at the timestamp check, before it even computes the HMAC. The endpoint's first decision after reading the body is `if (!verifier.IsValid(request, rawBody)) return Results.Unauthorized();`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **400 Invalid webhook payload**: that message is used only when the verified body deserializes to null.
- **200 because the HMAC is valid**: the timestamp check runs first and fails.
- **403**: the endpoint never returns Forbid; it uses Unauthorized.

excerpts.quote: return Results.Unauthorized();

notes.title: Both sides are lowercased before the comparison
notes.body:
**Key: yes, since both sides are lowercased before they are compared.**

The expected signature is `Convert.ToHexString(hmac.ComputeHash(payloadBytes)).ToLowerInvariant()`, and the header value is `signatureValues.ToString().Trim().ToLowerInvariant()`. An uppercase hex header becomes the same lowercase string, so the UTF-8 bytes passed to FixedTimeEquals are identical.

Why the others are wrong:
- **FixedTimeEquals compares exactly**: it does, but on the already-lowercased strings.
- **Base64 only**: the note and the code use hex.
- **Re-signs the uppercase form**: nothing is re-signed; the HMAC is computed once over timestamp.body.

excerpts.quote: var actual = signatureValues.ToString().Trim().ToLowerInvariant();

notes.title: Constant-time comparison defeats timing attacks
notes.body:
**Key: its run time does not depend on where the bytes first differ.**

An ordinary equality check stops at the first mismatching character, so a response arrives slightly sooner when an early byte is wrong. By measuring many requests an attacker can guess a valid signature one character at a time. CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals examines every byte of equal-length inputs regardless of mismatches, removing that signal.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Ignores case**: case-insensitivity comes from the two ToLowerInvariant calls.
- **Faster**: it is designed to be predictable, not faster.
- **Decodes the hex first**: the code passes UTF-8 bytes of the hex strings, not decoded HMAC bytes.

excerpts.quote: return CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(

notes.title: No event store means a retry runs again
notes.body:
**Key: the result is applied again, adding another Payment row.**

The endpoint deserializes the payload, calls engine.ApplyPaymentResult and returns `new { received = true, payload.EventId, payload.EventType }`. EventId is only echoed; nothing records it. With no Idempotency-Key header, IdempotencyMiddleware passes the request straight through. ApplyPaymentResult then saves the invoice as Paid again with a new PaidAt, adds another Payment and enqueues another outbound webhook, without checking the current status.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Replay by eventId**: no code looks up eventId.
- **409 for a seen event**: there is no record of seen events to conflict with.
- **Skipped because Paid**: ApplyPaymentResult has no status guard.

excerpts.quote: return Results.Ok(new { received = true, payload.EventId, payload.EventType });

notes.title: No header, no idempotency
notes.body:
**Key: it calls the next middleware straight away, so the handler runs again.**

After confirming the request is an unsafe /api method, InvokeAsync tries to read the Idempotency-Key header. When it is missing, it awaits next(context) and returns, with no hashing, caching or lookup. Each retry therefore runs the pay handler again. The architecture note's status box says requests without the header bypass the middleware entirely.

Why the others are wrong:
- **400 for a missing header**: the 400 is only for a key of the wrong length.
- **Replay by body hash**: the cache is keyed by method, path and key; without a key there is no entry.
- **409 for a repeated body**: 409 needs an existing entry under the same key.

excerpts.quote: if (!context.Request.Headers.TryGetValue("Idempotency-Key", out var idempotencyKeyValues))

notes.title: Keys must be 8 to 200 characters
notes.body:
**Key: it returns 400, since the key is under 8 characters.**

The middleware trims the header and checks `idempotencyKey.Length is < 8 or > 200`. abc123 has six characters, so it writes a 400 with the error "Idempotency-Key must be between 8 and 200 characters." and returns without calling the handler.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Cached for 24 hours**: caching happens only for valid keys after a 2xx response.
- **Padded**: nothing modifies the key besides Trim.
- **Ignored**: an absent header is ignored; a present but invalid one is rejected.

excerpts.quote: await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new { error = "Idempotency-Key must be between 8 and 200 characters." });

notes.title: Same key, different body: 409
notes.body:
**Key: a 409 saying the key was reused with a different payload.**

The cache key is method, path and Idempotency-Key, so the second request finds the stored entry. The middleware then compares the entry's RequestHash, a SHA-256 of method, path and body, with the new one; the bodies differ, so it writes 409 with "Idempotency key reused with a different request payload.". This matches the architecture note.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Replayed**: replay happens only when the hashes match.
- **A fresh run**: the lookup is by key, not by body, so the entry is found.
- **400, keys are single-use**: reusing a key with the same body is allowed; it replays.

excerpts.quote: error = "Idempotency key reused with a different request payload."

notes.title: Only successful responses are remembered
notes.body:
**Key: the handler runs again, because only 2xx responses are cached.**

After next(context) returns, the middleware copies the buffered response to the client and then stores it only `if (context.Response.StatusCode is >= 200 and < 300)`. A 400 is not stored, so the identical retry finds no entry and goes to the handler again. The status box in the architecture note states this limit.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The 400 is replayed**: there is no entry to replay.
- **409 for a used key**: 409 needs a stored entry with a different hash.
- **400 from the middleware**: the middleware only produces 400 for a key of the wrong length.

excerpts.quote: if (context.Response.StatusCode is >= 200 and < 300)

notes.title: Check, run, then store: a race window
notes.body:
**Key: both run the handler, since nothing is stored until a response exists.**

Each request calls store.TryGet at line 35 and finds nothing. The entry is written by store.Set only after `await next(context)` completes and the status is 2xx. In between, nothing marks the key as in progress, so both requests reach the handler. The lock in IdempotencyStore makes each dictionary call thread-safe, but it is released before the handler runs.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The second waits on the lock**: the lock covers only TryGet and Set, not the handler.
- **409 because the key is reserved**: nothing reserves the key; the status box says so.
- **A replay**: there is nothing to replay until the first response is stored.

excerpts.quote: if (store.TryGet(cacheKey, out var cached))

notes.title: The cache key includes method and path
notes.body:
**Key: a normal run of its handler, since the cache key includes the path.**

The middleware builds `cacheKey = $"{context.Request.Method}:{context.Request.Path}:{idempotencyKey}"`. POST:/api/customers:key and POST:/api/plans:key are different entries, so the second request finds nothing and runs normally. Its request hash also includes the path, but the lookup fails before any comparison.

Why the others are wrong:
- **409**: a 409 requires an entry under the same cache key.
- **Replay of the customers response**: the entries are separate.
- **400 for a non-unique key**: the only 400 is for key length.

excerpts.quote: var cacheKey = $"{context.Request.Method}:{context.Request.Path}:{idempotencyKey}";

notes.title: Round to whole cents, then normalise the currency
notes.body:
**Key: 2000 minor units in USD, with the midpoint rounded away from zero.**

FromMajor computes `decimal.Round(amount * 100m, 0, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero)`: 19.995 * 100 is 1999.5, which rounds to 2000. It then calls the constructor, which sets Currency to NormalizeCurrency(currency), that is Trim().ToUpperInvariant(), so " usd " becomes USD.

Why the others are wrong:
- **1999, truncated**: decimal.Round rounds; nothing truncates.
- **Currency kept as given**: the constructor always normalises it.
- **1999.5 kept**: MinorUnits is a long, and the value is rounded before the cast.

excerpts.quote: var minor = decimal.Round(amount * 100m, 0, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero);

notes.title: A late failure can reopen a paid invoice
notes.body:
**Key: it goes back to Open, with a failed Payment added.**

ApplyPaymentResult builds `succeeded ? invoice with { Status = Paid, PaidAt = now } : invoice with { Status = Open }` and saves it, then records a Payment whose status follows the event. It never reads the invoice's current status first, so a payment.failed event after success moves a Paid invoice back to Open. Because events are not deduplicated or ordered, a delayed or replayed failure can do this.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Nothing changes**: there is no guard on the current status.
- **Void and reversal**: no Void transition or reversal exists on this path.
- **409**: the endpoint returns 200 unless the invoice id is unknown (400).

excerpts.quote: : invoice with { Status = InvoiceStatus.Open };

notes.title: Reading the docs2 guide: data, access and quality pages
notes.body:
The newer questions in this quest come from the longer `docs2/` learning guide that sits next to the two short design notes. Five pages are used:

1. `03-architecture-and-patterns/02-data-model-and-persistence.md`: the entity diagram, where each entity lives in `BillingStore`, the query table, the section on multi-write operations, and the schema-change rules for a future database.
2. `03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`: what is validated at each endpoint, then the sections on authentication, authorization and what adding them would take.
3. `05-quality-engineering/05-security-checklist.md`: the scored table and the pre-merge list.
4. `05-quality-engineering/01-testing-strategy.md`: test levels, seams, flake sources.
5. `05-quality-engineering/06-observability-and-operations.md`: signals that exist and a starter list.

The guide often contrasts how this in-memory app behaves today with what a database-backed or production version would need. As you read, keep two columns: *today* and *after the move*. Many questions ask which column a statement belongs in, so open the code anchors the pages link to and check the today column yourself.

excerpts.quote: not as object references — which is exactly how they'd map to columns in a relational DB.

readMore.why: How the docs2 guide is organized into modules.
The in-memory store most of these pages describe.

notes.title: The database, not the app, enforces uniqueness
notes.body:
Today `AddCustomer` scans `_customers` with `.Any()` inside the store's single lock, so the check and the insert cannot interleave: O(n), but consistent. Move the data to a database and keep the same code, and the lock is gone: two concurrent inserts can both run the check, both see no match, and both insert. That is a **read-then-write race**, and the guide's fix is not more application code but **a unique constraint** on `Email` (and on plan and coupon `Code`).

- *Still safe under a lock*: the in-process lock does not exist across database connections or instances.
- *Cache every email in memory*: a cache is one more copy that can race.
- *Retry around `.Any()`*: retrying a racy check is still a racy check; only the constraint can refuse the second insert.

excerpts.quote: it's a unique constraint. Knowing that the *database* enforces uniqueness, not the application

notes.title: GenerateInvoice is four writes, not one
notes.body:
In `BillingEngine.GenerateInvoice` the writes run in this order: `SaveInvoice`, `SaveUsageEvents` (stamping usage with the invoice id), `SaveSubscription` (advancing the period), then `EnqueueWebhook`. Each call takes the store's lock on its own, so each is atomic by itself, but the four are **not atomic together**. A crash after the first call can leave **an invoice saved while the subscription period never advances**, and later crashes leave other half-finished combinations.

- *One locked transaction*: there is no durable transaction boundary at all; the guide says so directly.
- *The shared lock makes all four atomic*: the lock is taken and released per call.
- *An outbox replays the invoice*: the webhook row is just the last of the four writes; nothing replays the operation.

Moving to a database makes the transaction boundary explicit and necessary.

excerpts.quote: In the in-memory world these are individually atomic (each `lock`) but not *collectively* atomic.
store.SaveInvoice(invoice);

notes.title: Immutable records, but last write still wins
notes.body:
Entities are immutable C# records, so an "update" is a new copy made with `entity with { … }` followed by an explicit `Save*`. `SaveInvoice` simply overwrites the dictionary entry by key. Immutability protects each copy, not the stored row: if two requests each build a copy from the same original and both save, **the later save overwrites the earlier one**, and there is **no optimistic concurrency** to notice. In a database you would add a `RowVersion`/`xmin` check here.

- *The later save fails on a version mismatch*: no version is stored or compared today.
- *Field-by-field merge*: the store replaces the whole record.
- *The lock makes the second re-read*: the lock covers only the save, not the read-modify-write cycle.

excerpts.quote: There is **no optimistic concurrency** — last write wins.

notes.title: Expand first, contract later
notes.body:
The guide's first two schema rules are the classic expand-then-contract pattern for changing a live database while old and new code both run:

1. **Additive first**: add the column as nullable (or a new table), deploy, backfill, and only then make it non-null. Adding a non-null column with no default in one step breaks existing rows and old writers.
2. **Rename = add + copy + drop, across releases**: add the new column, write both, migrate readers, then drop the old one.

- *Non-null in one step, rename in place*: exactly what the rules forbid.
- *A temporary default and a view*: not the guide's recipe; it backfills and writes both columns.
- *Nullable forever*: the rule ends by making the column non-null.

excerpts.quote: Add the new column, write both, migrate readers, then drop the old

notes.title: Decide the Money mapping before the first migration
notes.body:
`Money` is a value type with integer minor units and a currency code. A relational schema can store each money field as **two columns** (`MinorUnits`, `Currency`) or as an EF Core **owned type**. The guide calls this choice the trap because once rows exist in one shape, switching to the other means rewriting stored data: **a data migration, not a code change**. Decide it up front.

- *Guid key generation*: the guide does not discuss it; ids are already Guids.
- *Caching `Invoice.Lines`*: the separate rule about Lines is that it must become a child table or owned collection, since a list cannot be one column.
- *Partitioning usage*: not mentioned.

excerpts.quote: Changing that decision later is a data migration, not a code change.

notes.title: Presence checks let bad values through
notes.body:
The endpoints check that input is *present*, not that it is *sensible*. Create customer only rejects a blank name or email, so an email of `"x"` **is accepted**. Record usage only rejects a quantity of zero or less, so a two-billion-unit event **is accepted** too, and the next invoice is absurd. The guide files both under the R-12 gaps, along with a currency that is only uppercased.

- *Both rejected*: there is no email-format check and no upper bound on quantity.
- *Quantity capped at the plan's limit*: plans carry prices, not usage caps, and nothing caps the event.
- *Email rejected*: only presence is checked.

The broader lesson: validation for shape and range is a different job from authorization.

excerpts.quote: **Email format isn't validated** — only presence
**Usage quantity has no upper bound**

notes.title: One signature is not an auth system
notes.body:
NetBilling registers no authentication at all: no `AddAuthentication`, no `[Authorize]`, no JWT or cookie handling. The webhook HMAC is the only credential-like check, and it proves that a request came from **the payment provider, on one endpoint**. It says nothing about users. So **every endpoint under `/api` is anonymous**.

- *User sessions and 401s*: no sessions exist, so nothing returns 401 for a missing login.
- *A merchant API key on writes*: no API keys are issued or checked.
- *SPA origin and CORS*: CORS controls which browser origins may read responses; it is not authentication, and any non-browser client ignores it.

excerpts.quote: which authenticates *the payment provider* on one endpoint — not users.

notes.title: When the id is the only key, every endpoint is an IDOR
notes.body:
No entity has a `TenantId` or `OwnerId`, so the API cannot tell whose invoice is whose. `POST /api/invoices/{id}/pay` therefore lets **any caller pay any invoice, given only its Guid**. The guide generalizes: every id-bearing endpoint is an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference), because possession of the id is the only requirement.

- *The owner's session cookie*: there are no sessions or cookies.
- *An admin role claim*: there are no claims or roles; the handler checks none.
- *The owner's Idempotency-Key*: that header only deduplicates retries; it is not a credential.

Guids are hard to guess, but they leak through URLs, logs and shared screenshots; unguessable is not the same as authorized.

excerpts.quote: the only thing you need to act on someone else's resource is its `Guid`.

notes.title: Identity from claims, ownership checked on lookup
notes.body:
The guide's four-step design for adding auth starts with where identity comes from: the caller's identity and tenant come **from validated claims**, never from the request body. `TenantId` is then set on every owned entity from the principal, and every store query is scoped by tenant. For ids in the URL or body, **look the resource up and verify it belongs to the caller**; returning 404 rather than 403 often hides that the resource exists.

- *Tenant id in the body* or *a tenant header from the SPA*: both are values the caller controls, so a caller could simply claim another tenant.
- *Trust the URL id once signed in*: being authenticated says who you are, not that this invoice is yours.

excerpts.quote: The caller's identity (and tenant) comes from validated claims, never from the request body.
Look the resource up *and* verify ownership

notes.title: Authorization needs one boundary, not many checks
notes.body:
Authorization is a rule that must hold on **every** path that touches owned data: a **cross-cutting invariant**. If each endpoint adds its own check, the next endpoint someone writes can forget it, and per-endpoint bolting guarantees a miss sooner or later. The guide's answer is **a single boundary that cannot be bypassed**: an authorization filter, or tenant scoping baked into the store so an unscoped query is impossible to write.

- *Wait for the database migration*: the boundary is a design choice, not a storage feature.
- *Check only writes*: reads leak data too; the dashboard already returns everyone's data.
- *Per endpoint behind feature flags*: still per endpoint, which is what the guide says will miss one.

excerpts.quote: a boundary (a filter, or scoping baked into the store) that's impossible to bypass.

notes.title: No cookies today, so no CSRF surface yet
notes.body:
Cross-site request forgery works by getting a victim's browser to send a request that **automatically carries their cookies**. NetBilling sets **no cookies and has no sessions**, so there is nothing for a forged request to ride on, and the checklist marks CSRF *mostly N/A*. The condition is spelled out: **if you add cookie auth, you must add anti-forgery**.

- *CORS blocks origins; JWT bearer needs anti-forgery*: CORS is a separate row, and a bearer token in a header is not sent automatically by the browser, so it is not the case the row warns about.
- *React escaping*: that is the XSS row.
- *All routes are GETs*: the API has many POST endpoints.

excerpts.quote: **If you add cookie auth, you must add anti-forgery.**

notes.title: SSRF waits for the first real outbound call
notes.body:
Server-side request forgery means tricking your server into calling a URL the attacker chose, such as an internal admin service. Today the webhook worker **simulates** delivery and never makes the HTTP call, so the checklist marks SSRF *N/A today*. Once delivery is real, the target comes from `WebhookEvent.Destination`, which the checklist calls **attacker-influenced**, so destination URLs must be validated or allowlisted.

- *No URLs stored, fixed provider host*: every event already stores a destination URL.
- *CORS keeps it safe*: CORS governs browsers calling this API, not this API calling out.
- *Only admins can set URLs*: there is no authentication, so there are no admins.

excerpts.quote: the destination is attacker-influenced (`WebhookEvent.Destination`) — validate/allowlist URLs or it's an SSRF vector.

notes.title: A committed default secret is a shared secret
notes.body:
The webhook signing secret has a default value, `dev_secret_replace_me`, **committed to `appsettings.json`**. Anyone who can read the repository can sign webhooks that the verifier accepts, unless every deployment remembers to override it. The checklist's fix (R-09) has two parts: **move the secret to the environment or a secret store**, and **fail fast in production** so a missing override stops startup instead of silently using the default.

- *Env var without rotation*: the value is in a committed file, not read from the environment.
- *Stored hashed*: an HMAC key cannot be hashed; the verifier needs the raw key.
- *Shipped in the SPA bundle*: the front end never sees it; the problem is the repository.

excerpts.quote: Move to env/secret store; fail fast in prod.
"WebhookSigningSecret": "dev_secret_replace_me",

notes.title: No tests yet, and where to start
notes.body:
The testing-strategy page opens with the current state: **there is no test project and no test anywhere** (risk R-03, verified by file listing). It then sizes a plan to this repo. The **highest-value 80%** is **unit tests on the engine**, made deterministic by the injected clock, plus **a thin layer of `WebApplicationFactory` integration tests** for validation, status codes and idempotency replay. UI and end-to-end tests come later for a single-screen app.

- *A unit or integration project exists*: neither does.
- *Playwright and React tests first*: the page explicitly ranks UI and E2E lower.
- *Contract plus E2E suite*: contract checks are manual today, and E2E is one smoke test, later.

excerpts.quote: unit tests on the engine (deterministic via the clock) + a thin layer of `WebApplicationFactory` integration tests.

notes.title: Seeded dates move unless the clock stands still
notes.body:
`BillingStore` seeds itself in its constructor by calling `Seed(clock.UtcNow)`, and the seed builds dates such as `now.AddDays(-30)`. So the seed dates are **relative to the moment the store is constructed**. With a fixed `IBillingClock` they are identical on every run; with the system clock they shift each run, and any test asserting a specific date flakes. Hence: **use a fixed clock in tests**.

- *Hard-coded calendar dates*: they are computed offsets, not literals.
- *Random on each run*: the GUIDs are fixed and the dates follow the clock; nothing is random.
- *Relative to the first request*: they are computed at construction, before any request.

excerpts.quote: the seed uses `now.AddDays(-30)` etc. relative to construction time

notes.title: Drive workers directly and isolate the store
notes.body:
Two of the flake sources in the table come from how the app is wired. The workers run on a `PeriodicTimer` (4 s and 8 s); a test that waits for a real tick is slow and timing-dependent, so **call `Process`/`Deliver` directly** or drain the queue synchronously. The store is a singleton, so tests sharing one `WebApplicationFactory` mutate the same data; **build a fresh factory per test class** or reset state between tests.

- *Wait out a real tick*: that is the timing dependence the row warns against.
- *Shrink the interval*: still a real timer, and non-parallel classes would still share one store.
- *Mock the timer and sort results*: sorting is the separate ordering row, and a shared factory still shares state.

excerpts.quote: don't wait on the real timer — call `Process`/`Deliver` directly, or drain the queue synchronously
build a fresh factory per test class, or reset state between tests
